title: Lessons from Silicon Valley Bank
summary:
Maintaining solvency requires bank management to be aware of the riskiness of the assets they
acquire, among other things. Thus, you minimize your costs by borrowing for a day or a month, but you expose yourself
to the risk of rising interest expense since you haven't fixed your rate for long. But that subjects you to the risk of capital losses if interest rates rise.

reader_summary.headline: This isn't going to be another history of the meltdown of Silicon Valley Bank.
reader_summary.overview: This isn't going to be another history of the meltdown of Silicon Valley Bank. Dozens of those have appeared in my inbox over the past month, as I'm sure they have in yours. Thus, rather than merely recount the developments, I'm going to discuss their significance.

key_points.text: My sense is that the significance of the failure of SVB and signature bank is less that it portends additional bank failures.
key_points.evidence_quote: My sense is that the significance of the failure of SVB and signature bank is less that it portends additional bank failures, and more that it may amplify pre-existing wariness among investors and lenders, leading to further credit-tightening and additional pain across a range of industries and sectors.

key_points.text: One-off or a harbinger of things to come.
key_points.evidence_quote: One-off or a harbinger of things to come.

key_points.text: A number of things about SVB made it somewhat of a special case.
key_points.evidence_quote: A number of things about SVB made it somewhat of a special case, which means it probably won't turn out to be the first of many.

key_points.text: The bank's business was heavily concentrated in a single sector.
key_points.evidence_quote: The bank's business was heavily concentrated in a single sector.

thesis: The failure of Silicon Valley Bank was a special case driven by its unique concentration in volatile sectors, its specific asset-liability mismatch involving long-dated bonds, and its high leverage, rather than a sign of widespread systemic problems in the U.S. banking system. However, the episode highlights universal banking risks inherent in borrowing short to lend long, high leverage, and reliance on depositor trust, which can lead to insolvency if confidence is lost during rising interest rate environments.
